name_en: Uzumi — vegetables and seafood hidden beneath rice, ladled with broth
summary_ja: 里芋やえび、鯛などをだしで煮て椀に入れ、上からご飯を盛って隠す福山の料理。江戸時代、贅沢を控えるため具をご飯の下に埋めたのが始まりと伝わる、秋の実りを祝う一皿である。
summary_en: Simmered taro, shrimp, and sea bream sit in a bowl hidden under a mound of rice in this Fukuyama dish. It is said to date to the Edo period, when diners tucked good ingredients beneath plain rice to appear modest, and it later became a way to mark the autumn harvest.

name_en: Mobiri — rice mixed with simmered root vegetables and black beans
summary_ja: 広島の方言「もぶる（混ぜる）」に由来する混ぜご飯。ごぼうやしいたけ、黒豆を炊き込み、農作業の合間や祝い事の際に大きなおむすびにして近所へ配る風習が大竹市などに伝わっている。
summary_en: Named for the Hiroshima dialect word "moburu" (to mix), this rice is tossed with simmered burdock, shiitake, and black beans. In Otake and nearby towns it was formerly rolled into large rice balls and handed out at farm breaks and celebrations such as house-raisings.

name_en: Taimeshi — whole sea bream cooked into rice by Seto Inland Sea fishermen
summary_ja: うろこと内臓を取った鯛を丸ごと釜に入れ、米と炊き込む瀬戸内の漁師料理。岩礁の多い海底と潮流が鯛の産卵に適し、約380年前に始まったという鞆の浦の鯛しばり網漁とともに伝わってきた。
summary_en: A whole sea bream, scaled and gutted, is set into the pot and cooked together with the rice—a fisherman's dish from the Seto Inland Sea. The area's rocky seabed and currents suit bream spawning, and the dish is tied to the roughly 380-year-old tai-shibari net fishery of Tomonoura.

name_en: Kinako musubi — rice balls with pickled plum, dusted in toasted soy flour
summary_ja: 梅干しや塩吹き昆布を包んだおむすびにきなこをまぶす、田植えの合間の一品。ユネスコ無形文化遺産「壬生の花田植」で今も振る舞われ、丸く握るのは秋の豊作への願いと伝わる。
summary_en: Rice balls stuffed with pickled plum or salted kelp are dusted thickly in toasted soybean flour, eaten during breaks from rice planting. Still served at the Mibu no Hanataue festival, a UNESCO-listed rice-planting rite, the round shape is said to carry a wish for a bountiful autumn.
source_title: きなこむすび 広島県

name_en: Takomeshi — rice cooked with octopus, a fisherman's meal from Mihara
summary_ja: 漁師が船上でぶつ切りのたこを飯に炊き込んだのが始まりという三原の料理。速い潮流にもまれて足が太く締まる三原沖のたこを、ごぼうやにんじんとともにだしじょうゆでじっくり炊き込む。
summary_en: Fishermen once chopped up freshly caught octopus and cooked it right into their rice on board—the origin, it is said, of this Mihara dish. Fast currents off Mihara give the octopus thick, taut legs, and the meat is simmered into rice with burdock and carrot in a soy-seasoned broth.

name_en: Ebamaki — nori rolls of rice and Hiroshima-na pickle for seaweed fishermen
summary_ja: ご飯に広島菜漬けとかつおぶし、白ごまをあえ、焼きのりで巻いた江波地区ののり巻き。片手で漕ぎながら食べられるよう両端を閉じることもあり、のり漁師の船上食として広まったと伝わる。
summary_en: Rice is tossed with Hiroshima-na pickle, bonito flakes, and sesame, then rolled in toasted nori—a roll from Hiroshima's Eba district, long known for seaweed cultivation. The ends are sometimes tucked shut so it can be eaten one-handed while rowing, a food born for nori fishermen working on the water.

name_en: Gyohan — flaked grilled fish and rice topped with a bone-based broth
summary_ja: 焼いてほぐした白身魚と錦糸卵、えびなどをご飯に盛り、その骨でとっただしをかけて食べる竹原の料理。塩田で栄えた町の「浜旦那」がもてなしに用いた膳が、途絶えかけたのち文献で再現されたと伝わる。
summary_en: Flaked grilled white fish, egg crepe, and shrimp are arranged over rice, then doused in a broth made from the fish's own bones—a dish from Takehara, a town once wealthy on salt production. Nearly lost, it was reconstructed decades later from an old newspaper clipping after salt farming ended.

name_en: Kaki meshi — rice cooked with Hiroshima Bay oysters and root vegetables
summary_ja: 酒でいりつけた牡蠣を、にんじんやごぼう、油揚げとともにだしで炊き込む江田島の炊き込みご飯。うまみをたっぷり蓄える12〜2月の牡蠣が特においしいとされ、駅弁としても親しまれている。
summary_en: Oysters, seared briefly with sake, are cooked into rice together with carrot, burdock, and fried tofu in this dish from Etajima, an island known for oyster farming. The oysters are said to taste richest from December to February, when they store the most flavor-giving glycogen.

name_en: Anago meshi — grilled conger eel laid over broth-cooked rice at Miyajima
summary_ja: かば焼きにしたあなごをそぎ切りにし、だしで炊いたご飯に敷き詰める宮島の一皿。速い潮流にもまれて脂がのる「瀬戸のあなご」を使い、明治34年に宮島口駅の駅弁として売られたのが始まりと伝わる。
summary_en: Conger eel, grilled kabayaki-style, is sliced and layered over rice cooked in dashi—a dish from Miyajima. It uses "Seto anago," prized for the fat that fast currents help build into the fish, and is said to have begun in 1901 as a bento sold at Miyajimaguchi station.
